## In short

Proactive communication is reaching out to customers and prospects when nothing is wrong. Installed as a team's daily habit, it compounds into sales you can forecast.

Credentials: CEO of Outgrow. Outgrow Certified Advisor. YPO member. Founder since 2005. Works across the US, UK and India.

He helps $50M–$500M businesses replace reactive selling with proactive daily disciplines, with a target of 15–30% predictable annual revenue growth. Outgrow was founded by Alex Goldfayn. ## Speaking

One keynote, built from doing the work.

The talk comes from the Outgrow method and 20 years of building and scaling businesses. There is no theory and nothing recycled from someone else. Sid shows a room how proactive selling works, and what to do differently on Monday.

### The keynote

Outgrow: How to Expand Market Share and Outsell Your Competition

Most companies wait for the phone to ring. This talk shows a room where their next block of revenue is actually sitting, and the small daily habits that bring it in. Audiences leave with moves they can start using the same week.

- Rooted in the Outgrow methodology, not general sales theory
- Built from 20 years in the founder seat
- Shaped for the room, whether that is a conference or one leadership team
- Delivered across the US, UK, India and internationally

Formats:

- Conference keynote. Conferences and industry events.
- PE portfolio days. For investor-backed management teams.
- Leadership offsites. Shaped for one leadership team.
- Media. Podcast and media guest appearances, including HoldCo Builders Podcast and First Time Founders Podcast. Recent podcasts: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/podcasts

As of September 2026 there is one keynote, titled above. Sid previously offered three separate keynote titles.

## About

Walked the path. Now he guides others through it.

Sid Jashnani is the CEO of Outgrow and a London-based Outgrow Certified Advisor. He helps leadership teams install proactive selling as a daily habit, aiming to compound it into 15–30% predictable sales growth, every year. Sales doing, not sales training.

Sid has been a founder since 2005. He scaled a systems integration business across the IT infrastructure ecosystem to £27M+ revenue. Along the way he lived the inconsistent quarters, the delegation gaps, the cash-flow pressure, and the daily firefighting most founders know too well.

Then he came across Outgrow, Alex Goldfayn's methodology. The insight was straightforward: operational excellence alone doesn't drive growth. Proactive communication does. Reaching out to customers and prospects when nothing is wrong. Sid installed the habit inside his own teams, watched it compound, and became an Outgrow Certified Advisor.

Today Sid is CEO of Outgrow, the company Alex Goldfayn founded, where he helps Alex execute the vision. His role is to bring clarity, consistency and commercial discipline to the business, and to support Outgrow's advisors and clients across the world. He also works directly with mid-market leadership teams across the US, UK and India.

Figures shown on the page:

- £27M+ revenue scaled in his own businesses
- 15–30% is the target annual growth from the Outgrow habit, not a guaranteed result
- Founder since 2005
- Three geographies: US, UK, India

## Advisory

Outgrow Advisory: install the habit, track it, let it compound.

A structured engagement to install the Outgrow system inside a business. The team makes a handful of proactive communications a day. It is tracked weekly. For mid-market businesses generating $50M–$500M in annual revenue.

1. Diagnose the growth constraint. Identify whether the revenue gap is a behaviour problem (reactive selling, founder dependency) or a product-market fit issue.
2. Install proactive disciplines. Replace hope-based selling with daily proactive outreach to existing customers and warm relationships.
3. Create accountability cadences. Simple tracking and team rituals that make proactive selling a daily discipline, not an occasional effort.
4. Measure and compound. Track proactive activity and revenue outcomes weekly, so the habit builds year after year.

What a client is working towards:

- Reach out to customers and prospects when nothing is wrong, as a daily habit
- Remove the revenue dependency on the founder or any one seller
- A target of 15–30% predictable new sales growth a year, tracked weekly
- Works alongside any operating system already in place

### Outgrow Workshop

A full day with the client's sales managers and salespeople. The team learns how Outgrow works, practises it on the client's real customers, and leaves knowing what to do on Monday morning. In person across the US, UK and India, or online.

This workshop was previously called The Proactive Sales Sprint. The name changed in September 2026. The audience is sales managers and salespeople.

### Outgrow Sprint

A six-week online programme from Outgrow. A team learns alongside people from other companies, with three live working sessions and three office hours, and uses the method on its own customers as it goes. Dates: https://runoutgrow.com/sprint/

The Outgrow Sprint is an Outgrow programme, not a service Sid Jashnani delivers personally. Sid is CEO of Outgrow.

## Questions answered on the page

### Who is Sid Jashnani?

Sid Jashnani is a keynote speaker, the CEO of Outgrow and a London-based Outgrow Certified Advisor. He helps mid-market leadership teams install proactive selling as a daily habit, with a target of 15–30% predictable sales growth every year. He works across the US, UK and India, is a YPO member, and has been a founder since 2005. Outgrow itself was founded by Alex Goldfayn; Sid is its CEO and helps Alex execute the vision.

### What does Sid speak on?

Sid delivers one keynote: Outgrow: How to Expand Market Share and Outsell Your Competition. It shows a room where their next block of revenue is sitting and the daily habits that bring it in. He speaks at conferences, industry events, PE portfolio days, leadership offsites and in the media, across the US, UK, India and internationally.

### What is the Outgrow Workshop?

The Outgrow Workshop is a full day with your sales managers and salespeople. The team learns how Outgrow works from start to finish, sees why doing the work matters more than knowing about it, and practises the habits that bring in new sales on real accounts. Everyone leaves with tools they can use the next morning. Sid runs it in person across the US, UK and India, or online.

### What is the Outgrow methodology?

Outgrow is a revenue growth methodology that installs simple, proactive customer communication behaviours into a business. It replaces reactive, hope-based selling with repeatable daily disciplines, aiming for 15–30% predictable annual revenue growth. The focus is on existing relationships, not new lead generation. Sales doing, not sales training.

### Who does Sid work with?

Mid-market businesses generating $50M–$500M in annual revenue across Technology, SaaS, Professional Services, Insurance, Distribution, Manufacturing and Healthcare, primarily in the US, UK and India. Outgrow works best when the product is proven and the growth constraint is behaviour, not product-market fit.

## Your moat is thinner than you think

- Date: 20 October 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/your-moat-is-thinner-than-you-think/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/your-moat-is-thinner-than-you-think

# Your moat is thinner than you think

- Date: 20 October 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/your-moat-is-thinner-than-you-think/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/your-moat-is-thinner-than-you-think
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

What would stop your best customer from leaving tomorrow, or from buying from someone else next week?

## First, what is a moat?

A moat is whatever protects a business from its competitors, like the ditch round a castle. Warren Buffett made the picture famous, writing in his 1995 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, “In business, I look for economic castles protected by unbreachable ‘moats.’” It is why a customer can’t easily walk across the road to someone else: a price nobody can match, a brand people trust, or a product that is very hard to build.

![Image from the essay “Your moat is thinner than you think”](https://sidjashnani.com/assets/blog/your-moat-is-thinner-than-you-think/3558dfe3fb666791.webp)

## Why AI has made technical moats so much weaker

Software used to be protected by the years and the big team it took to build. AI coding tools are wearing that away, and the clearest recent case involves Adobe.

On 3 October 2026, Brandon Thomas, founder of ArtCraft, posted on X, “I’ve vibe coded replacements to 7 of Adobe’s apps in Rust. They’re open source.” The seven include lookalikes of Photoshop, Illustrator and Premiere. Ars Technica reports he used Claude Opus 5.5 and calls them clean-room rewrites, meaning written without Adobe’s code. The Photoshop and Premiere repositories were both created on 30 September, and Photoshop’s first release is dated 2 October, so in public at least this took days, not years.

![Image from the essay “Your moat is thinner than you think”](https://sidjashnani.com/assets/blog/your-moat-is-thinner-than-you-think/d16d6cd35e330edc.webp)

It is far from finished. Thomas calls the apps “super early alpha”, the Photoshop project’s own roadmap puts it at about 45 percent ready for real work, and testers on Hacker News were split on whether it works. What strikes me is how cheap the first copy has become.

Nikita Bier made the same point on X on 12 October 2026, saying technical moats are mostly over, and that for something meant to last, the only moats left are proprietary data, network effects and a physical component.

![Image from the essay “Your moat is thinner than you think”](https://sidjashnani.com/assets/blog/your-moat-is-thinner-than-you-think/a0c25d3c28579bf3.webp)

## The moat is usually thinner than we think

Most of us reach for quality or service, which is what the next supplier will say, so here is where I’ve landed. For most businesses I come across, there is little or no moat beyond helping customers get value and keeping them happy. I have tried hard to argue myself out of that view and can only partly.

Some mid-market businesses do have a real moat, such as painful switching, a contract that runs for years, or so many engineers or sites in one area that a newcomer struggles to match you. Others have a specialist skill that takes years to learn, or a licence that regulation makes hard to get. If you have one, protect it, but be honest about whether you have it or just wish you did.

## What the moats thread left standing

Later that day, levelsio quoted Nikita’s post and widened the list to include audience and distribution, capital, and regulatory barriers. Both are about building technology companies, so don’t stretch them.

![Image from the essay “Your moat is thinner than you think”](https://sidjashnani.com/assets/blog/your-moat-is-thinner-than-you-think/bac3e635b9e74dce.webp)

Neither list says “customer relationships”, but in my view a customer list is a kind of proprietary data and a kind of audience. A competitor with the same tools can’t copy that by next Tuesday.

## A relationship only counts if you tend it

Happy customers still leave. They drift, or someone rings them with a better price, or nobody ever asked them for more.

> **A moat protects the revenue you have. It doesn’t go and find you more. Behaviour does.**

When I explain this, a common reply is that calling customers after they’ve used what they bought is already part of their process. I said that’s great, and asked, “Who is doing it?” There was absolute silence, because I think nobody or hardly anybody was. A line in a process document is a different thing from someone picking up the phone this week.

Customers mostly call us when something is wrong, so a call when nothing is wrong tends to surprise them.

**That is where Outgrow starts. Outgrow is a revenue growth system that helps companies grow revenue 15 to 30 percent a year, organically and systematically. It starts with current customers, then past customers, prospects, past prospects and referrals. So start there: call your current customers when nothing is wrong.**

Private equity leaders seem to agree that growth is where the work is. Kearney’s April 2026 survey of 100 US private equity leaders found 69 percent named revenue growth and commercial excellence as a most critical operating lever today, ahead of AI and working capital. That is what they say matters, not proof it works, and it is revenue, not EBITDA.

## The first three things to say

The call takes about two minutes. Start like this.

1. “I was just thinking about you. How are things with the family?” If they ask whether something is wrong, tell them, “No, I’m just calling to check in on you.”
2. “How was the experience?” Ask this after they have used what you sold them, and then listen.
3. “Do you know we also do [one other thing you offer]?” Customers often see you as one thing only. If you want to go further, ask, “What else is going on in your world? Is there anything I can help you with?”

Then agree when you will speak next. That one call, made when nothing is wrong, is the start of how a business grows without chasing strangers.

I continue to build Outgrow’s UK practice, working with owners and with PE and operating partners who want organic revenue growth from the customers they already have. If that’s you, I’d be glad to connect. And if you’re curious about becoming an Outgrow advisor, say hello.

**Sources**

- [Berkshire Hathaway 1995 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1995.html), dated 1 March 1996
- [Brandon Thomas on X](https://x.com/echelon/status/2106387247234752762), 3 Oct 2026
- [Ars Technica, “Software is over”: Bold AI developer takes aim at Adobe with open source clones](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/10/software-is-over-bold-ai-developer-takes-aim-at-adobe-with-open-source-clones/), Kyle Orland, 7 Oct 2026
- [PhotoCraft](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft), its [roadmap](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/main/docs/roadmap.md), and [FilmCraft](https://github.com/storytold/filmcraft)
- [Hacker News thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49958850)
- [Nikita Bier on X](https://x.com/nikitabier/status/2109497987055640958) and [levelsio on X](https://x.com/levelsio/status/2109653584706990506), both 12 Oct 2026
- [Kearney, “Private equity’s new rules of engagement: why operational alpha is the only durable response”](https://www.kearney.com/industry/private-equity/article/private-equitys-new-rules-of-engagement-why-operational-alpha-is-the-only-durable-response), survey of 100 US private equity senior leaders, April 2026, published 4 Jun 2026

## “I’ll call them after lunch.” They never do.

- Date: 6 October 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/ill-call-them-after-lunch-they-never/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/ill-call-them-after-lunch-they-never

They know a call works. They feel like they are bothering someone.

# “I’ll call them after lunch.” They never do.

- Date: 6 October 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/ill-call-them-after-lunch-they-never/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/ill-call-them-after-lunch-they-never
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

They know a call works. They feel like they are bothering someone.

People will tell you a phone call is better than an email, and then they will not make the call. In workshops I hear the same line. Someone says they will ring after lunch, because it is about two o’clock and the customer might be in a meeting. What they usually mean is that they feel like they are bothering someone.

I worked with an after school activity provider that was packed before and during the summer. They took the bookings that came in, and they did not sell beyond that. Summer was the moment to put winter packages in front of parents and book the quiet months while people were already saying yes. They did not do it. When winter came and the phones went quiet, they complained, fixed their website, hired a lead gen agency, bought Instagram ads so the phone might ring. The names were already in the address book. All they had to do is dial it in.

> **Outgrow is the doing. You make the call because you are helping, not bothering. If they are busy, you leave a voicemail or a voice note and follow it with a text. There is a very high statistical probability (we exactly know…) that they will communicate back with you.**

Then you count the calls, so day three and beyond does not turn into an excuse.

If you want a written reply on whether 15–30% systematic organic growth looks realistic for your business for next year, connect and I will send you five questions.

You will have the reply within five working days. If it is not a fit, you still get the reply.

## No Activity, No Revenue

- Date: 21 September 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/no-activity-no-revenue/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/no-activity-no-revenue

When the diary falls apart, the very first thing founders drop is the only thing that actually feeds the pipeline.

# No Activity, No Revenue

- Date: 21 September 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/no-activity-no-revenue/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/no-activity-no-revenue
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

When the diary falls apart, the very first thing founders drop is the only thing that actually feeds the pipeline.

My luggage was stuck somewhere in transit, the calendar for the rest of the week was completely derailed, and an in-person revenue growth workshop was still waiting for me to be delivered.

![Image from the essay “No Activity, No Revenue”](https://sidjashnani.com/assets/blog/no-activity-no-revenue/ffd5e190d16adca6.webp)

My immediate instinct, which is probably the same instinct most of us have when things go wrong, was to start complaining. I wanted to blame the airport management, the weather, and the ground crew, giving myself full permission to write off the entire afternoon. But as I opened my notepad to list the things I needed to get done, I glanced at a short reminder I had posted down few weeks ago during another messy week.

**It simply said that complaining about a lack of results is usually just an excuse to hide from the activity that creates them.**

That note stung, mostly because it brought back a very specific, very uncomfortable memory from when I had first moved across the Arabian sea to live in Dubai.

![Image from the essay “No Activity, No Revenue”](https://sidjashnani.com/assets/blog/no-activity-no-revenue/e62cfbfdf63d4e2d.webp)

I had convinced myself that I had reached a stage in my career where the standard rules of commercial legwork no longer applied to me. I started suffering from what I now call Elite Surgeon Syndrome. I thought of myself like a top specialist on Harley Street, someone who sits quietly in a private consulting room while clients queue up down the hall, wait their turn, and politely ask for an appointment.

Because I believed I was above the basic, unglamorous work of picking up the phone and following up, I completely stopped doing it. I told myself that outbound follow-up was undignified, that my reputation would carry the load, and that serious people wait for inbound demand.

Meanwhile, living costs and the monthly business burn rate remained entirely real. Dubai is an expensive place to entertain delusions. The hunger slowly evaporated, but the overheads did not. It took an uncomfortably long time, and a painful amount of burned cash, to admit the truth to myself. I was not operating like an elite specialist. I was just hiding behind my ego because I thought I had outgrown the basics.

**Whenever revenue stalls in a business, founders almost always look for complicated explanations.**

They tell themselves they have a positioning issue, or an offer structure problem, or that the market needs a completely new strategic narrative. What is actually happening is much simpler and much harder to face. When the diary blows up, or when a good year whispers in your ear that you have arrived, the very first thing you drop is the daily commercial legwork.

That drift is human, and I know how easily I slip into it myself. It is genuinely the main reason Outgrow exists in my working life today. Alex Goldfayn created the system, and when I stepped in as CEO of Outgrow LLC, it was not because I thought I had solved sales forever. It was because I needed an operating system that would protect me from my own complacency.

![Image from the essay “No Activity, No Revenue”](https://sidjashnani.com/assets/blog/no-activity-no-revenue/5bcd5cedd483a944.webp)

At its heart, the Outgrow methodology is a disciplined, weekly rhythm of proactive outreach to people you already know. You reach out to existing clients and past relationships before they ask. You look for ways to be genuinely useful to them, you track your swings honestly, ask for referrals, and you stay humble enough to pick up the phone week after week. Not through clever tricks, but through pure consistency.

Do not spend Sunday tweaking your deck or rewriting your website copy.

**Shrink your horizon right down to today. The work will still feel unglamorous, but your pipeline will start moving again.**

Happy Selling,

Sid

CEO, Outgrow LLC

## Why “we’ll run it internally” almost never gets run

- Date: 15 September 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/why-well-run-it-internally-almost/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/why-well-run-it-internally-almost

Two questions: why haven’t you done this before, and what will be different going forward?

# Why “we’ll run it internally” almost never gets run

- Date: 15 September 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/why-well-run-it-internally-almost/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/why-well-run-it-internally-almost
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

Two questions: why haven’t you done this before, and what will be different going forward?

Two hours into the session. The whiteboard is covered. The leadership team is nodding along, agreeing with every single point.

Then the owner leans back in his chair:

“This is great. But honestly, I think we can just run this ourselves.”

Nobody in that room is lying.

They are smart, capable people. They have a CRM. They have weekly leadership meetings. They have a competent sales manager. On paper, there is zero reason they could not build and install the entire operating rhythm tomorrow morning.

Yet they almost never do.

> **Over the years, I learned never to argue when an owner says that. Arguing turns the room into a contest, and you never win a contest with a founder in their own boardroom.**

Instead, I ask two simple questions.

> **First: “Why haven’t you done this already?”**

Then I stop talking.

The honest answer usually surfaces after a short pause. We have been busy firefighting. We talked about doing it last Q4. We kicked off an initiative two years ago, but daily client demands took over and it drifted.

Then comes the second question.

> **“What is actually going to be different this time?”**

That is the uncomfortable one.

Because the person assigned to enforce the daily outreach, hold people accountable to the call log, and inspect the inputs is the exact same person who has to sit next to them at lunch tomorrow.

When accountability is internal, grading gets soft.

A team member misses their daily calls for three days straight because an operational fire broke out. The manager lets it slide because they understand the stress. By week three, proactive calls become optional again. By month two, the entire system has quietly evaporated into the background.

I once watched a single division inside a mid-market distributor attempt to run the playbook entirely on their own. That one division managed about 20% growth because the department head was unusually stubborn.

The rest of the business? Completely flat.

Same company. Same materials. Totally different execution.

Nobody grades their own homework honestly. Not because people are malicious or lazy, but because we naturally protect workplace harmony over awkward compliance conversations.

> **Artificial harmony only causes problems.**

The issue was never capability.

“We can do this ourselves” is rarely a strategy.

More often, it is an unconscious admission that everyone likes the idea of the result, but nobody inside the building wants the daily friction of enforcing the standard.

## We found $4M in his existing customers in 45 minutes

- Date: 8 September 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/we-found-4m-in-his-existing-customers/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/we-found-4m-in-his-existing-customers

No new market. No new product. No new hires.

# We found $4M in his existing customers in 45 minutes

- Date: 8 September 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/we-found-4m-in-his-existing-customers/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/we-found-4m-in-his-existing-customers
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

No new market. No new product. No new hires.

I sat with a friend who runs a $7M business and in 45 minutes we found $4M he didn’t know he had.

No new market. No new product. No new hires. Just his existing customers.

Here’s what we did. I asked him to list his top customers by revenue. Then his middle tier. Then his smallest accounts. Then I asked for two more lists: prospects he’d quoted in the last two years and lost, and customers who’d stopped buying.

Five segments. Took about fifteen minutes to build.

Then I asked one question for each segment.

For the top tier: “What else do you sell that they don’t buy from you yet?” He started listing services. Three of his biggest clients had no idea he offered two of his most profitable lines. They were buying those services from someone else. Not because they preferred the competitor. Because nobody had ever told them.

For the middle tier: “What would it take to move them up?” In most cases, one conversation. One proactive call asking what else they needed. That’s it.

For the smallest accounts: “Are any of these worth growing, or are they just filling your capacity?” He realised four of them were costing him money. Unprofitable work he’d never reviewed.

For the lost quotes: “Have you followed up since they said no?” He hadn’t. Not once. Some of those quotes were eighteen months old. The prospects’ situations had changed. Their budgets had reset. Nobody had called.

For the churned customers: “Do you know why they left?” He didn’t. Not for most of them. No exit conversation. No follow-up. They just stopped ordering and he assumed they’d found someone better.

> **Forty-five minutes. Five segments. $4M mapped on a single page.**

His response: “We can easily do 70% of what you’ve just put on this page.”

That’s $2.8M. From customers who already know him, already trust him, already have a relationship with him. No cold outreach. No ad spend. No new logo acquisition.

One common thing I hear from founders is “we need more leads.” And I always ask the same thing. What are you already sitting with?

Every customer you have can buy more from you. Every customer. We just don’t ask. Silence is not satisfaction. It’s just silence. And the money sitting inside your existing base will go to a competitor who does ask, eventually.

The work isn’t complicated. It’s a segmentation exercise and a series of phone calls. But it requires someone to actually pick up the phone and have the conversation.

> **As goes your actions, so goes your revenue.**

What percentage of your existing customers know about everything you sell?

Keep Selling,

Sid

-

## The Question Before the Pitch

- Date: 18 August 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/the-question-before-the-pitch/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/the-question-before-the-pitch

Why the best salespeople surface objections on purpose, before they even start selling.

# The Question Before the Pitch

- Date: 18 August 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/the-question-before-the-pitch/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/the-question-before-the-pitch
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

Why the best salespeople surface objections on purpose, before they even start selling.

What would be the reasons we're not going to move forward?

That's the question one of our Outgrow Certified Advisors opened with on a pre-proposal call last month.

Not "let me walk you through what we do." Not "here's how we've helped companies like yours." Not even "what are your goals this quarter?"

Just that one line. Before the pitch. Before the deck. Before anything.

And the room went quiet for about five seconds. Then the prospect said something no one expected.

"Honestly? We've been burned before. We hired a consulting firm last year that promised transformation and disappeared after 90 days. So my biggest concern is that this is going to be another one of those."

Four minutes into the call, the real blocker was on the table. Not budget. Not timing. Not "we need to talk to our board." The actual thing that would have quietly killed the deal three weeks later came out in the first conversation.

Here's why this works.

Most salespeople treat objections like obstacles. Something to overcome. Something to handle. They prepare scripts for "too expensive" and "we're happy with our current provider" and "send me some information." They rehearse comebacks.

But the best salespeople don't handle objections. They invite them.

When you ask someone why they wouldn't move forward before you've even started selling, two things happen.

First, the prospect feels safe. You're not pushing. You're not pitching. You're asking them to be honest, and you're doing it before they have any reason to put their guard up. That changes the entire energy of the conversation.

Second, you get to build your entire proposal around the thing that actually matters. Instead of guessing what matters, instead of leading with features and hoping something sticks, you know exactly what to address. Your pitch becomes a direct answer to their deepest concern.

The advisor on that call didn't panic when the prospect said "we've been burned before." He didn't rush to differentiate. He just said, "Tell me more about what happened." And for the next ten minutes, the prospect told him everything. The bad experience. The broken trust. The specific things that would need to be different this time.

By the time the advisor started talking about Outgrow, he wasn't selling anymore. He was responding to a specific problem with a specific solution. The prospect had already told him exactly what to say.

> This is what proactive selling actually looks like. It's not about being pushy. It's not about volume. It's about asking better questions earlier than anyone else is willing to.

Most people wait for objections to surface on their own. They hope they won't come up. And when they do, usually in week three of the sales cycle when the deal is about to close, everyone scrambles.

The question before the pitch eliminates that scramble. It pulls the future into the present. It lets you deal with reality instead of assumptions.

Try it on your next call. Before you open your deck, before you share your screen, before you do anything, ask: "What would be the reasons we wouldn't move forward?"

Then be quiet. Let them answer. And build everything that follows around what they tell you.

Hit reply and tell me the objection you keep hearing too late. I'll tell you the question that surfaces it in the first five minutes.

## You already have the customers. You just have a small share of each one.

- Date: 11 August 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/you-already-have-the-customers-you/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/you-already-have-the-customers-you

Revenue growth and execution discipline for leaders who are done with guessing.

# You already have the customers. You just have a small share of each one.

- Date: 11 August 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/you-already-have-the-customers-you/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/you-already-have-the-customers-you
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

Revenue growth and execution discipline for leaders who are done with guessing.

I ran a business to £27M and never once asked a customer what percentage of their spend came to me.

Not once. I could have told you what every account was worth to the pound. I had no idea what that pound was a fraction of.

Nobody teaches you to ask. It feels faintly rude, like asking somebody what they earn.

Then one of our Outgrow advisors told me about a distributor. $14M one year, $25.5M the next. No acquisition, no new sales hires, roughly the same list of customers as before. What changed is that the people who had spent a decade taking orders started ringing people instead.

I found that super interesting when I first heard it and reflected back on the time when I was running my system integration business. What irritated me was that the growth was sitting there the whole time, and reason nobody collected it was not the market, which I often blamed when things were not looking too rosy.

---

## The question

Pick your tenth biggest customer. Not the top one. You are far too invested in the top one to be honest about it.

Now answer this: what share of everything they spend in your category comes to you?

Most founders cannot. They know the invoice. They have never gone and found the denominator.

So they have been treating a 12% relationship and a 90% relationship in exactly the same way for years, and only one of those has any room left in it.

I sat with an owner last year who worked out he had about a tenth of an account he had been calling “ours” since 2011. He wasn’t cross with the customer. He went quiet, and then said, nobody has ever asked them.

Loyal is not the same word as exclusive. Loyal usually means they keep buying the thing they have always bought from you and get everything else somewhere down the road.

---

## How to actually ask it

Not a survey. On a call, in a normal voice, the way you’d ask anything else.

“Roughly what share of your spend in this category comes our way at the moment?”

Then shut up.

People answer it far more easily than you would expect. It costs them nothing, and being asked flatters them slightly.

Then the follow up, which is the one that actually pays:

“What would have to be true for that to be a bigger number?”

You are not selling now. The buyer is telling you, in their own words, exactly what sits between you and the rest of their budget. Sometimes it’s price. More often it’s that they had no idea you did the other thing.

That’s the part that still gets me. A good chunk of what people are chasing on a Sunday night is sitting behind a sentence nobody said out loud.

---

## What it looks like when someone actually runs it

A talent and professional services business had five flat years and then put on $900K of new growth, 18% in five months. A copier and IT services firm did 20% in half a year. An IT company nearly tripled its count of new customers in the first month, which I would treat with some suspicion if I hadn’t watched the same shape happen elsewhere.

None of them found a new market. They went and asked the people who were already paying them.

---

## Why it won’t happen on its own

Because “ask your customers what share you’ve got” is advice. Advice does not survive a Tuesday.

Somebody has to decide who gets asked this week. Somebody has to write down what they said. And somebody has to look at that list on Friday, notice that four of the eleven never happened, and say something about it, which is the bit everyone quietly skips.

That is what **Outgrow** is. A sales operating system. Sales doing, not sales training. Prescribed daily behaviours, five to ten minutes a person, logged, looked at every week, done by everyone who touches a customer rather than only the people with sales in the job title.

You don’t need more customers to grow 15 to 30% next year. You need more of the ones already picking up the phone to you.

I got to £27M without knowing that. I have no idea what it cost me and I have stopped trying to work it out.

What share of your best customer’s spend do you actually have, and when did anybody last ask them?

## Train the frontline and you get a good week. Train the manager and you get a good year.

- Date: 4 August 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/train-the-frontline-and-you-get-a/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/train-the-frontline-and-you-get-a

Stop installing your revenue system in the wrong place.

# Train the frontline and you get a good week. Train the manager and you get a good year.

- Date: 4 August 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/train-the-frontline-and-you-get-a/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/train-the-frontline-and-you-get-a
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

Stop installing your revenue system in the wrong place.

Most founders install a new sales habit at the frontline.

They gather the sellers. They teach the behaviour. Everyone nods. It works for a fortnight. Then it fades.

Not because the people are weak. Because the habit had nobody to hold it.

Alex Goldfayn put a number on this that I keep coming back to. Working with managers is roughly 80/20 more impactful than working with the frontline. Same effort, four times the return, because a manager doesn’t do the behaviour once. A manager multiplies it across a team, every week, for as long as they run the team.

Teach a seller and you’ve changed one person’s Tuesday. Teach a manager to run the system and you’ve changed how forty people work for a year.

## What the manager actually holds

The behaviour survives because someone runs a weekly huddle around it. Not a status meeting. A short, repeatable rhythm with four parts.

Review the scorecard. Who did the proactive work last week, who didn’t, what did it produce.

Share the wins. Read out a real one. A dormant customer reopened, a quote chased down, an order size that grew. Wins are contagious, and they teach faster than instruction.

Prescribe the customers. Name who each person calls this week. Not “make some calls.” These customers, by name.

Prescribe the products. Point at what to talk about, so the calls have a purpose beyond checking in.

Fifteen minutes. Every week. Same shape.

## The one rule that holds it together

Always connect the actions to revenue. Never track actions in isolation.

The moment a huddle becomes “did you make your calls,” it dies, because it feels like surveillance. When it stays “here’s the revenue those calls opened,” it lives, because everyone can see the point.

That’s the difference between a manager policing activity and a manager leading growth.

## Why founders get this wrong

Because the frontline is where the selling looks like it happens. So that’s where the attention goes.

But the frontline is where the behaviour is done. The manager’s chair is where the behaviour is kept alive. Install it there and it compounds. Install it below there and you’re re-teaching it every month until you give up and call the system a failure.

It wasn’t the system. It was the level you installed it at.

**Outgrow is built to live in the manager’s weekly rhythm. Sales doing, not sales training. The frontline makes the calls. The manager makes sure next week they still do.**

## The close

A seller can give you a good week.

A manager who runs the rhythm gives you a good year.

Who in your business is actually holding the weekly rhythm your revenue depends on, and what happens to it the week they stop?

## The one question that turns "really keen" into money.

- Date: 21 July 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/the-one-question-that-turns-really/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/the-one-question-that-turns-really

They said yes. So why isn't it a sale?

# The one question that turns "really keen" into money.

- Date: 21 July 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/the-one-question-that-turns-really/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/the-one-question-that-turns-really
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

They said yes. So why isn't it a sale?

**“Yes, this makes complete sense.”**

You’ve heard it. It feels like the finish line.

It isn’t. A yes without a date is just a nice feeling you both had in a room. And feelings cool.

So after the yes, I ask one question.

“When would you like to launch?”

If they give me a date, wonderful. It goes in the calendar and the deal has somewhere to live.

If they don’t, I don’t retreat. I climb down the ladder.

No date? “Which month are you picturing?” No month? “This quarter or next? Before the summer or after?” No quarter? “Is this a this-year decision, or a next-year one?”

Each rung asks for less. Each rung still asks for something.

### Why this works

The power is not the information. It’s the commitment the question raises.

A prospect who says “September” has done something the prospect who says “soon” hasn’t. They’ve pictured it. They’ve put it on a mental calendar. They’ve made it real to themselves, in their own words, out loud.

And here is what I’ve watched happen more than once. A client starts growing revenue the moment they decide to run Outgrow. Before the launch. Before the first prescribed call. The decision itself changes how the team shows up on Monday, because now there is a date, and a date organises behaviour the way a wish never does.

### The prospect who genuinely can’t start yet

Sometimes the timing is real. They can’t begin for months.

Fine. Offer to hold the slot. A small deposit secures the date.

Framed right, that’s a gift to them, not a hoop for you. They plan around it. They’ve committed to their own calendar, not just to a warm chat with you.

### The mistake I made for years

I treated the yes as the close.

So I’d send a friendly “just checking in,” get a friendly “still keen,” and six weeks later the warmth had faded to nothing. Nobody said no. The deal just never had a date to stand on.

Interest decays. A date does not.

Outgrow runs on commitments, logged and reviewed, not on good feelings remembered.

### The close

A yes tells you they like it. A date tells you they’ll do it.

Which deal in your pipeline is “really keen” with no date on it? That’s not a win yet. That’s your next call.

## THE COMMITMENT LADDER

After the yes, get a date. If you can’t get a date, get a rung. Ask the top rung first, then climb down one step at a time until they commit to something.

**1. Date** — “When would you like to launch?” → a calendar entry; the deal has somewhere to live. **2. Month** — “Which month are you picturing?” → they’ve placed it in real time. **3. Quarter** — “This quarter or next? Before summer or after?” → a window you can plan and follow up against. **4. Year** — “Is this a this-year decision, or a next-year one?” → the truth about how real it is.

**The rule:** the power isn’t the information you gather. It’s the commitment the question raises. Saying “September” out loud does something “soon” never will.

**For the prospect who genuinely can’t start for months, the deposit move:**

> “Sounds like the timing is a few months out. Want me to hold the slot for you? A small deposit secures the date so you can plan around it.”

Framed as their benefit, not your hoop. They commit to their own calendar.

A yes tells you they like it. A date tells you they’ll do it.

Interest decays; a date does not.

Sid Jashnani | sidjashnani.com | sidjashnani.substack.com

## Referrals aren’t luck

- Date: 7 July 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/referrals-arent-luck/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/referrals-arent-luck

Stop waiting for referrals. Start asking for them.

# Referrals aren’t luck

- Date: 7 July 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/referrals-arent-luck/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/referrals-arent-luck
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

Stop waiting for referrals. Start asking for them.

**Referrals aren’t luck. They’re a question nobody asks.**

Every founder loves a referral.

Warmest lead there is. Half sold before the first call. The cheapest pipeline in the business.

And almost nobody asks for them on purpose.

We treat referrals like weather. Something that happens to us. A nice surprise when it lands, a quiet disappointment when it doesn’t.

Here is the truth. Your happiest customer right now knows two or three people who should be buying what you sell. People in their world. People with the same problem you just solved for them.

They would introduce you gladly.

You have just never asked.

## Why we don’t ask.

It feels needy.

You did good work, the client is happy, and something in you says don’t push it. Don’t spoil it. Don’t look like you need it.

That is the same voice that kills proactive selling everywhere. The fear of being a bother.

So flip it round.

You are not asking for a favour. You are giving someone you have helped the chance to help someone they care about. You solved a real problem for them. There is a person in their network with that exact problem, losing sleep over it right now. The introduction is a gift in both directions.

See it that way and the ask stops feeling like begging.

## The ask, made specific.

“Do you know anyone who might need me?” gets you nothing. It is too big. The brain goes blank.

Make it small and specific.

“Who else do you know who is dealing with the exact thing I just fixed for you?”

“You said you are happy with how this went. Is there one person you would feel comfortable introducing me to?”

One problem. One person. Easy to answer.

## Why it has to be systematic.

One referral ask is easy. Remembering to ask, every time, across everyone who touches a customer, is hard. That is where it falls apart. It gets left to the moments people happen to feel brave.

So you stop leaving it to chance.

In Outgrow, the referral ask is a prescribed action. Scripted, assigned, logged, and reviewed every week alongside the proactive calls and the “did you know” questions. It gets counted like every other swing, because we know the batting average. Ask enough happy customers, and a predictable share say yes.

[Outgrow. The sales operating system that makes the rest of the stack do what it was supposed to do.](http://runoutgrow.com)

Luck becomes a number you can grow.

## The shift.

Stop hoping your best customers send people your way.

Start asking them, on purpose, every week.

Who is the one happy customer you could ask this week, and whose name do you think they would give you?

-

Sid Jashnani

Outgrow Certified Advisor™,

CEO of Outgrow

sidjashnani.com | sidjashnani.substack.com

## You didn't overpay. You under-committed.

- Date: 23 June 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/you-didnt-overpay-you-under-committed/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/you-didnt-overpay-you-under-committed

Why the thing you bought to grow became the thing you resent

# You didn't overpay. You under-committed.

- Date: 23 June 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/you-didnt-overpay-you-under-committed/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/you-didnt-overpay-you-under-committed
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

Why the thing you bought to grow became the thing you resent

There’s a particular way to waste money that almost nobody warns you about.

It isn’t buying the wrong thing. It’s buying the right thing and going half-in.

I see it with founders all the time. They invest in something real. A system, a process, a way of working that genuinely moves revenue. They mean it when they sign. And then the week happens.

The system needs twenty minutes a day. They give it twenty minutes when there’s nothing more urgent, which is never. It needs a weekly rhythm. They run it for two weeks, miss one, then quietly stop.

Six months later they look at what they spent and feel cheated.

But the system didn’t fail them. It was never switched on.

Here’s the line I keep coming back to. Anything worth doing becomes a very expensive hobby the moment you go half-in.

A gym membership you use twice a month is the most expensive way to not exercise. A CRM nobody updates is the most expensive way to forget your customers. And a growth system you run when you feel like it is the most expensive way to stay exactly where you are.

The cost isn’t the invoice. The cost is paying for the outcome and not collecting it.

## Why Not Now?

- Date: 12 June 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/why-not-now/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/why-not-now

How a text message forced me to stop coaching around the problem and start solving it.

# Why Not Now?

- Date: 12 June 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/why-not-now/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/why-not-now
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

How a text message forced me to stop coaching around the problem and start solving it.

A client sat across from me, furious.

“We’ve done all of this and we’re back to square one.”

ICP built. Playbook done. Comp plan in place. Months of work. And not a single deal moved.

That conversation kept happening. Different client, same words.

Eventually I had to admit the thing I’d been stepping around for years. I was coaching everything except the thing that mattered most. Sales.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗳𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗽

For years I had a business that worked. Good clients. Good conversations. Two, maybe three days a week of real work.

Comfortable. And that was the problem.

Because in every quarterly review, the same thing surfaced. The top line wouldn’t move. Coaching only works when there’s demand. And as markets got crowded, demand stopped being a given.

Sales solves a lot of problems. When it’s firing, the operational noise quiets down. When it isn’t, everything gets louder. More frustration. More blame. People stop adding to the pipeline and start clinging to what’s left.

I could see the problem in every business I worked with. I just couldn’t fix it.

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗹 𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗱

It was from Alex Goldfayn. An invitation to see what his system, Outgrow, could do inside a practice like mine.

I’d read the lots of sales books. Every one of them told you how to think about selling. How to handle the objection, how to structure the team.

None of them showed you how to actually do it.

Outgrow did. It was the doing.

The decision in front of me was simple. Get certified in January, or wait until April.

Naturally, I picked April. A bit more time. A bit more runway. Get a few things in order first.

It was a lie. The same “later” I’d watched a hundred clients hide behind.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁

Then Alex sent a message.

“Why not now? What’s stopping you from helping yourself and your clients make more money? Do you think it’ll be that different in April?”

I read it a few times. It landed because it was true. I was letting life happen to me. Waiting for a better moment that was never going to announce itself.

Twenty years has taught me this: if you’re not sure where you’re going, you’ll still end up somewhere. But if you know exactly where you’re going, the path gets easier. The waiting is just fog.

I booked January.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗸𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

I told my wife it was a big investment. Significant. She asked the obvious question. Why this, why now.

So I talked her through the whole thing. Sales is the number one problem for the people I work with. Solve sales and you fund everything else. You give a business the budget and the breathing room to fix the rest.

She listened. Then she said, “Yeah, that makes sense. You need sales to grow.”

I needed to hear myself say it out loud as much as I needed her to agree. By the end of that conversation, I wasn’t apprehensive anymore. I was certain.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁

I flew to Chicago. Got certified. Rebuilt my practice around one thing instead of ten.

The first three months were uncomfortable. New language. New rhythm. Calls I hadn’t made in years.

But by the end of those three months, I’d closed three clients.

From a standing start. From a business I’d just decided to blow up because it was too comfortable.

Most growth doesn’t die from a bad decision. It dies in the gap between deciding and doing.

So let me leave you with the question Alex left me with.

That hire you’re waiting on. That system you’ll implement next quarter. That conversation you keep putting off.

Why not now?

— Sid

Outgrow Certified Advisor.

CEO at Outgrow LLC.

Twenty years building businesses and a lot of lessons that cost more than they should have.

## Your CRM is not your sales system. Here is what is...

- Date: 2 June 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/your-crm-is-not-your-sales-system/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/your-crm-is-not-your-sales-system

A CEO sat across from me last month and said: “I’ve got a sales team.

# Your CRM is not your sales system. Here is what is...

- Date: 2 June 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/your-crm-is-not-your-sales-system/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/your-crm-is-not-your-sales-system
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

A CEO sat across from me last month and said: “I’ve got a sales team.

A CEO sat across from me last month and said: *“I’ve got a sales team. A CRM. A methodology my last consultant left behind. And a coach who shows up every quarter. So why does my revenue still wobble?”*

I told him what was missing.

He stared at me. Then he said: *“Why does no one talk about this?”*

That’s the post.

---

**The stack everyone has. The part nobody can name.**

Walk into any £5M+ business and you’ll see the same stack.

A sales team. A CRM. A methodology the team got trained on two years ago. A coach who flies in once a quarter. A pipeline review every Friday that everyone half-attends.

And revenue still wobbles.

Quarter to quarter. The forecast is a guess dressed up as a number. Good months feel like luck. Bad months feel like a personal failing.

I’ve been in those rooms for twenty years. First as a founder building a £27M business. Next as a business coach that would fly in to facilitate quarterly planning sessions and now as the CEO of an organisation that’s implemented this work across five hundred companies.

The pattern is so consistent it stopped being interesting and started being useful.

**Here’s the thing nobody names.**

Every good business has a **business operating system**. It’s how they run meetings. Set priorities. Hold people accountable. The CEO can describe it in two sentences.

Ask the same CEO what their **sales operating system** is. You’ll get a list.

*“We have a CRM.”*

*“We have a sales playbook.”*

*“We just hired a head of sales.”*

*“We did training last year.”*

None of those are a sales operating system. They are inputs. Tools. Assets. They sit around the system that doesn’t exist yet.

> A CRM records what happened. It doesn’t create what happens next.

Sales training tells your team what to say. It doesn’t change what they do on Tuesday at 10am when they have ten minutes between meetings and they have to choose between making a proactive call or refreshing their inbox.

A coach can light a fire. They cannot implement a daily behaviour across 22 customer-facing people who will quietly opt out the moment the coach leaves the room and does not follow up till next quarter.

The category is missing.

**Here’s what it looks like when you implement Outgrow® Sales Operating System.**

I worked with a founder last quarter who told me his sales team makes 200 calls a week. Revenue was flat.

I asked him how many of those 200 calls were proactive. Calls his team initiated. Not responses. Not renewals. Not reactions to a problem.

He didn’t know. Nobody in his business did.

We added one number to the weekly scorecard. Proactive calls per person.

Four weeks later that number was 38. The team had been calling. They had just been **responding**, not **initiating**. The behaviour that drives growth was missing. Nobody could see it until we counted it.

I call this **behaviour blindness**. It is the gap between activity and revenue, hiding in plain sight on every dashboard that only counts what already happened.

A sales operating system closes that gap.

**What a sales operating system like Outgrow® actually does.**

It treats every customer-facing person as a revenue role. Service techs. Project managers. Account managers. Customer success. Not just the sales team.

It runs on behaviours, not pipeline. We track what people do, not what they hope. Behaviours are leading. Pipeline is lagging. By the time pipeline tells you something is wrong, it already is.

It builds in the support that humans actually need. Mindset coaching every week. Relaunches built into year two and year three because the work will fade. That is not a deficiency. That is the nature of asking humans to take extra actions. Every methodology that has pretended otherwise has watched its implementation die or wither after novelty wears off.

**The CEO objection.**

*“We already have a CRM. We already have a sales team. Why do I need another thing?”*

You don’t need another thing.

You need the thing all those things are sitting around but never quite become.

A CRM is a filing cabinet. A sales team is a group of people. A methodology is a slide deck. None of them, alone or together, install the daily behaviour that makes 15 to 30 percent of growth predictable.

**Outgrow® does.**

The category is missing. So I’m naming it.

---

**The question to sit with.**

If I asked your top ten customers what proactive contact looks like from your business in the last 90 days, what would they say?

Not the call when something went wrong. Not the renewal call. The contact where you reached out to ask what else you could help with. No agenda. Nothing was wrong when you called them.

Most CEOs already know the answer.

That answer is the size of the gap.

That gap is where the Outgrow® goes.

---

Sid Jashnani CEO,

Outgrow LLC

Outgrow Certified Advisor

sidjashnani.com | sidjashnani.substack.com

## Every time growth stalled, I hired. It took me years to see why it never worked

- Date: 24 May 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/every-time-growth-stalled-i-hired/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/every-time-growth-stalled-i-hired

The most expensive habit I had as a founder, and the system that finally replaced it.

# Every time growth stalled, I hired. It took me years to see why it never worked

- Date: 24 May 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/every-time-growth-stalled-i-hired/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/every-time-growth-stalled-i-hired
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

The most expensive habit I had as a founder, and the system that finally replaced it.

**The job spec I kept rewriting**

The quarter was soft. Pipeline thin. The number on the board was lower than it should have been, and everyone in the room could feel it.

I knew exactly what to do. We needed another salesperson.

So I wrote the job spec. Again.

I’d done it before. More than once. Revenue would wobble, and my first instinct was always the same. More feet on the street. A new hunter. Someone hungry who’d go and find the growth we were missing.

It felt like leadership. It felt like doing something. Writing that spec gave me the same relief a treadmill gives you. Movement that feels like progress.

We hired. We onboarded. We handed over a target and a Pipedrive CRM login and a quiet hope that this was the missing piece.

**What actually happened**

The new person worked hard. They were good. And six months later the number looked almost exactly the same, except now it carried a bigger salary line.

It took me longer than I’d like to admit to understand why.

The new hire didn’t inherit a system. They inherited a vacuum. There were no prescribed daily actions for them to run. **No sales operating system**. No rhythm of proactive customer conversations they were expected to have. No weekly accountability beyond “how’s the pipeline looking.” They were dropped into the same unstructured space as everyone else and told to go be brilliant.

So they did what everyone else did. They reacted. They chased what was loud. They said they were making progress.

I hadn’t added a salesperson. I’d added another person to a sales function that ran on individual brilliance (or lack of that) and motivation.

**The thing nobody tells you about hiring**

Hiring doesn’t fix a sales problem. It multiplies whatever you already have.

If your sales engine is a set of clear, prescribed, daily behaviours, then more people pours fuel on a fire that’s already burning. Every hire compounds.

But if your sales engine is “everyone sells in their own way and when they get around to it,” then every hire just scales that. You pay more money to spread the same disorganisation across more desks. You scale chaos.

Here’s the part that stung. I had built operating processes and systems into almost every other part of my business. There was a rhythm to how we ran our operations, finance, the leadership team. A clear plan on a page. The right people in the right seats. Numbers everyone could see.

**The one place I never built a system was the place the money actually comes from.**

**What I’d do now, before hiring anyone**

If I could go back, I wouldn’t write the job spec. I’d install a sales operating system first. **And for this I recommend Outgrow.**

It is less dramatic than it sounds. It is a small set of proactive customer conversations/actions, done every day, by whoever is doing sales or facing the customer (could be your project manager, account manager or even your delivery drivers). Calling existing customers before anything is wrong, just to ask what else you could help them with. Asking the questions that surface needs they haven’t mentioned. Reconnecting with the prospects you quoted and lost. Asking for the introduction you never get round to asking for.

A few minutes per person, per day. Logged. Reviewed once a week. Actually held to account, not just hoped for.

It works whether you are the only person selling or you have a full team. For the solo founder, it ends the feast and famine cycle of sell, deliver, look up, find the pipeline empty, start again. For the founder with a customer facing team, it turns a room of busy people into a predictable engine that doesn’t depend on who happens to feel motivated this week.

Get that running with the people you already have. Watch what the existing team produces when the work is structured.

Then, if you still need to hire, hire. You will be pouring fuel on something that already burns.

**The hard part**

The job spec is the easy decision. It feels like progress and it buys you a few months of hope.

The system is the harder decision, because it asks you to look honestly at what your current people are actually doing every day, and to admit the gap was never headcount.

I avoided that look for years. It was the most expensive thing I ever postponed.

So here is the question worth sitting with.

**Where is your revenue actually stalling?**

**Is it a people problem, or is it that the people you have were never given a system to run?**

Hit **reply** and tell me. If it is the second one, that is the most fixable problem in your business, and I will show you where I would start.

*Sid Jashnani*

*Outgrow Certified Advisor*

*CEO, Outgrow LLC · sidjashnani.com*

## Your top performers are watching how you handle the laggards

- Date: 17 May 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/your-top-performers-are-watching/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/your-top-performers-are-watching

The bottom third of your team will kill your growth system...

# Your top performers are watching how you handle the laggards

- Date: 17 May 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/your-top-performers-are-watching/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/your-top-performers-are-watching
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

The bottom third of your team will kill your growth system...

A founder called me last week. His revenue growth programme (Outgrow - it’s the best) had been running ten weeks.

The top of his sales team was on fire. New conversations. New opportunities. Customers being called for the first time in months.

But the numbers were uneven.

Some people were logging every day. Some were logging once a week. Some not at all.

He asked me what to do.

I asked one question.

“How many of your 22 customer-facing people are actually doing the work?”

He paused. Did the math.

“Maybe seven.”

About a third.

## Three thirds.

Every team I’ve ever installed a growth or coaching system into looks the same.

Top third does the work. Picks up the phone. Asks the DYK questions. Logs every call. Follows up before Friday. Their numbers move.

Middle third drifts. Means well. Was on a customer call. Will catch up tomorrow. Implements when reminded. Stops when the reminder stops.

Bottom third doesn’t do the work. Says “my customers don’t want to be called.” Says “we already have great relationships.” Says the system is “not how we sell here.”

They are the loudest voice in the team meeting.

That is the trap.

## The trap.

The founder was thinking about softening the cadence. Dropping the weekly logging. Letting the bottom third opt out of the daily calls.

To keep the peace.

I asked him what he wanted his sales team to look like in twelve months.

“Hitting our number.”

“No. What kind of people.”

“People doing the work.”

“Then why are you redesigning your system around the ones who aren’t?”

The room went quiet.

## Same shape. Different room.

This is not just an Outgrow problem. This is every system any founder or leader has tried to install.

The bottom third of your team takes the most management time and moves the fewest numbers.

The bottom third tells you the new system is “too much.”

The bottom third books a meeting with you to explain why their territory is different.

You can build your business around them.

Or you can build it around the top third.

You cannot do both.

## What I told him.

Three things.

**One.** Make the standard explicit. Write down what you expect every customer-facing person to do every day. The proactive calls. The DYK (Outgrow DYK) questions. The logged form. Most founders don’t, because it feels harsh. The cost of not writing it down is that everyone gets to interpret the standard differently.

**Two.** Tell them clearly. Sit each person down. “This is what doing the work looks like in this business now.” Most will surprise you. Some won’t.

**Three.** Move on quickly from the ones who won’t. Not in anger. Just quickly. Their seat is worth more than what they are putting into it.

## The cost of not doing it.

He knew this. Moving people on felt like he was failing them.

So I gave him the line.

You are not failing the bottom third when you move on.

You are failing the top third every time you don’t.

The top third are watching to see whether you will protect the standard or dilute it.

Dilute it and they stop logging too. Quietly. You won’t notice until you look up one day and the system has died across the whole team.

That is not a sales operation. That is a complaint line.

## What I am doing in my own work.

Same thing. Right now.

I am not extending advisory invitations to founders who book the call and “get busy” before the first session.

I would rather have ten clients doing the work than fifty looking at the system.

The bottom third can come back when they’re ready.

**In the meantime, I am rebuilding and growing revenue with people who are ready to do the work.**

That is the standard.

The number follows.

— Sid

Outgrow Certified Advisor

CEO, Outgrow LLC

## I Quit at Mile 3 of My Own Marathon

- Date: 10 May 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/i-quit-at-mile-3-of-my-own-marathon/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/i-quit-at-mile-3-of-my-own-marathon

The first marathon is the decision to change. The second is the one that actually counts. Most CEOs quit at mile 3.

# I Quit at Mile 3 of My Own Marathon

- Date: 10 May 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/i-quit-at-mile-3-of-my-own-marathon/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/i-quit-at-mile-3-of-my-own-marathon
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

The first marathon is the decision to change. The second is the one that actually counts. Most CEOs quit at mile 3.

I installed a daily huddle in one of my businesses years ago.

It worked. Then I killed it. Slowly. Without meaning to.

Every morning, 9am, 15 minutes. Quick numbers. Quick blockers. Who needs help with what. Faster decisions. Fewer fires. Less drift between teams.

Then I stopped showing up.

Not all at once. First it was a Tuesday I had to miss. Then a few days the week I was travelling. Then weeks at a time.

The huddle still happened. People still showed up.

Until they didn’t.

By the time I noticed, the energy had drained out of it. Conversations had gone shallow. The blockers stopped getting raised. Then the meeting itself stopped getting taken seriously.

And restarting it was harder than starting it the first time.

A few people quit during the relaunch. They weren’t high performers. They were the ones who’d been hiding behind weekly meetings. Daily made them visible. Visible made them uncomfortable. Uncomfortable made them leave.

That was the real cost. Lost momentum. A painful restart. People drifting out who I should have moved on years earlier.

All because I stopped showing up to a 15-minute meeting.

---

**THIS IS WHAT QUITTING AT MILE 3 LOOKS LIKE**

Today I run a different business. Daily huddle, every morning, no exceptions.

I see my old pattern in clients all the time.

They sign up for coaching, or an Outgrow programme, or any other meaningful change. They show up to the first session ready. They show up to the second one a bit tired. By the third or fourth, they’re looking for the exit.

The work didn’t get harder.

They just realised this isn’t a spa. It’s a gym.

Some came expecting a spa. They wanted to feel calm, validated, looked after. They didn’t want to lift anything heavy. They quit.

Some came thinking they were already fit. Then they showed up to a CrossFit class on day one and pulled something. They quit.

The ones who stay? They accept they’re going to be uncomfortable. They do the boring reps. They settle for singles and doubles instead of swinging for sixes every week.

Those are the people who grow 30, 40, 50, 100% over two or three years.

The quitters tell themselves the system didn’t work.

**The system worked. They stopped running.**

---

**WHAT GETS YOU PAST MILE 3**

Patience to follow the process when you can’t see results yet.

Persistence to keep showing up when it’s uncomfortable.

Perseverance to start again the day after you got it wrong.

Endurance to outlast every competitor who quits before you.

That’s the whole game.

The leaders who win aren’t the ones who started with the best plan. They’re the ones who stayed in the gym after they got sore.

I quit at mile 3 once.

I won’t do it again.

---

> What did you start three months ago that you’re already letting drift?

Tell me.

---

Sid

Sid Jashnani

CEO, Outgrow LLC

[Outgrow Certified Advisor](https://runoutgrow.com/advisor/sid-jashnani/)| [sidjashnani.com](http://sidjashnani.com)

## The 15-minute meeting that’s worth £5 million

- Date: 3 May 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/the-15-minute-meeting-thats-worth/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/the-15-minute-meeting-thats-worth

One of my companies doubled the revenue of another. Same product. Same market. The reason wasn’t what I thought.

# The 15-minute meeting that’s worth £5 million

- Date: 3 May 2026
- Mirror: https://sidjashnani.com/blog/the-15-minute-meeting-thats-worth/
- Original: https://sidjashnani.substack.com/p/the-15-minute-meeting-thats-worth
- Author: Sid Jashnani, CEO of Outgrow and Outgrow Certified Advisor
- Type: Letter

One of my companies doubled the revenue of another. Same product. Same market. The reason wasn’t what I thought.

I owned two companies in the same space.

Same product. Same market. Same opportunity sitting in front of both of them.

One did £10M that year. The other did £5M.

For a long time I was convinced the gap was talent. Then I was convinced it was timing. I floated the idea that one team had inherited the better client list. I told myself the other had a softer market.

None of it was true.

The only thing that separated those two businesses was discipline.

## What the £10M company did that the £5M company didn’t

The £10M company had a daily huddle. Scorecards reviewed every Monday. A weekly leadership meeting that nobody moved. The MD blocked time every fortnight to sit one-on-one with each of his managers, and he didn’t cancel them when things got busy. He didn’t cancel them when things got slow either.

Their meetings were boring. Predictable. Sacred.

When something went wrong, and things always go wrong in a growing business, the team was already on top of it. Decisions came fast because nobody was scrambling to catch up. They didn’t need an emergency meeting because they were never far from the data.

The £5M company did all of it ad-hoc.

Meetings happened when projects were lost. Reviews happened when cash got tight. Conversations happened when the shit hit the fan. Everything was reactive. Everything was a fire.

They had the fatter pipeline, by the way. They just couldn’t move it.

We tried to install the cadence. Weekly meetings, scorecards, one-on-ones, the whole stack. It didn’t take. They’re still in the same place today. Growing, but every extra pound feels like blood from a stone. Every win feels like it cost them three.

The £10M company is still growing. Still calm. Still boring.

## Then I saw the same pattern in a $2 billion business

Last week I was reminded of all of this.

A peer of mine runs an Outgrow programme inside a $2 billion company in the United States. He pulled the data on two of their branches.

Same brand. Same product. The same customers, literally the same customers, because the two branches are three miles apart and people stop at whichever one is on their way home.

Branch A runs weekly huddles. Branch B doesn’t.

Branch A is up 22% year on year. Branch B is down 11%.

That’s a 33-point swing. Three miles apart.

Same economy. Same market. Same buyers. Same brand.

The only variable is whether someone holds a 15-minute meeting on a Tuesday morning.

## Same lesson at every scale

The shape of what I saw in my own portfolio years ago is identical to what my peer saw last week inside a billion-dollar business.

> **Discipline isn’t a personality trait. It’s a calendar.**

The leaders who grow aren’t smarter, luckier, or better networked. They hold the meeting. They look at the scorecard. They have the awkward one-on-one. They do it on the slow weeks when nothing’s wrong, and they do it on the bad weeks when everything is.

The ones who don’t grow always have a reason. The market. The team. The product. The economy. The competitor.

It’s never the meeting they didn’t hold on Tuesday.

It’s always the meeting they didn’t hold on Tuesday.

## Run this audit yourself this week

Pick your best-performing unit. Branch, team, rep, region — it doesn’t matter. Then pick your worst.

Compare them on one thing only: cadence.

Are the meetings actually happening? Are the scorecards getting reviewed? Are the one-on-ones on the calendar, or are they getting pushed every week?

You’ll have your answer before you finish your coffee.

You don’t need a consultant for this one.

You just need to look.

---

Sid

*Sid Jashnani | Outgrow Certified Advisor* *[sidjashnani.com](https://sidjashnani.com) | [sidjashnani.substack.com](https://sidjashnani.substack.com)*
